title: The Hazard of Quartz Sand | Уралгрит
h1: The Hazard of Quartz Sand
text:
It is with regret that we note that some companies in the anticorrosion protection (ACP) industry still use quartz sand in their operations. In developed countries, a ban on the use of sand containing up to 90% silicon dioxide for anticorrosion works was introduced as early as the mid-20th century. In 1974, the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) issued a statement banning the use of quartz sand and other materials containing more than 1% free crystalline silica for surface treatment using abrasive blasting equipment. In the Russian Federation, the decree of the Chief Sanitary Officer G.G. Onishchenko prohibiting the use of sand for abrasive blasting operations has been in force since 2003.
The main danger of using quartz sand as an abrasive lies in the penetration of free crystalline silica particles into the lungs, leading to the occupational disease known as silicosis, commonly referred to as “sandblaster’s disease.” This is the most widespread and severe form of pneumoconiosis, caused by prolonged inhalation of dust containing free-form silica. It is a chronic disease that can lead to disability within a short period of time. Quartz sand contains 80–90% dust particles sized 5–10 microns, which form a dust cloud and negatively affect not only the sandblaster, but everyone within the work area. The human body attempts to clear these microscopic particles from the lungs by forming dense fibrous tissue, which significantly reduces the lungs’ ability to process oxygen.
The use of quartz sand as an abrasive material is not only dangerous to human health, but also insufficiently effective and may lead to corrosion in the near future.
Issues Associated with Surface Cleaning Using Sand
The rounded shape of sand particles results in the formation of a SHOT-type surface profile, which is unacceptable for certain types of paint and coating systems. It should be noted that sandblasting tends to polish the surface rather than remove corrosion to achieve the required surface profile.
Sand contains a high percentage of water-soluble salts (NaCl), which leads to the process of osmosis—blistering of paint and coating systems on the substrate. This ultimately causes coating failure.
Cleaning with quartz sand produces intense dust generation (2–4 times higher than when using slag abrasives). In an attempt to “save costs,” dust removal is often not performed, since sand is not easily visible on the treated surface. Even when dust removal is carried out, fine dust particles become embedded in the surface profile, disrupting the adhesion of the paint coating.
To ensure high-quality surface cleaning from rust, mill scale, and old paint coatings—while also providing safe working conditions—we recommend using modern non-granulated slag abrasives for abrasive blasting. You can purchase these materials at the best value from Uralgrit, a company that supplies modern surface preparation materials at affordable prices.

title: Surface Profile and Fractional Composition of Ungranulated Slag | Уралгрит
h1: Surface Profile and Fractional Composition of Ungranulated Slag
text:
Before applying a coating, it is necessary to ensure that the surface has the required degree of roughness.
By using an abrasive with a uniform fractional composition, it is possible to achieve the required surface roughness profile. This helps avoid unnecessary paint overconsumption and saves both time and money.
If the surface roughness profile is lower than specified, adhesion is negatively affected. If the profile is higher than required by the technical documentation, there is a risk that the profile peaks will not be fully covered during coating application, leading to localized corrosion points. Excessive profile height also increases the surface area, which in turn results in increased paint consumption.
A surface profile that meets project requirements allows the use of an optimal amount of coating, saving time and money. Careful control of surface roughness helps avoid excessive consumption of coating materials needed to cover profile peaks or costly repeat abrasive blasting to achieve the required profile depth.
The angular shape of the granules and the homogeneous fractional composition of Uralgrit abrasives make it possible to achieve a uniform surface profile in accordance with the customer’s specification.

title: Has Copper Slag Become Limited? Fact or Fiction? | Уралгрит
h1: Has Copper Slag Become Limited? Fact or Fiction?
text:
There have been increasing cases of unfair competition and misleading of consumers in the abrasive materials market, with facts being distorted regarding the exclusivity of copper slag production.
Copper slag, also known as copper smelting slag, is a “waste or by-product obtained during the smelting of copper from copper-bearing ore” (see Wikipedia).
In the USSR, copper-processing enterprises were located throughout the country, including the Southern and Middle Urals. Slag dumps formed as a result of copper smelting operations amount to tens of millions of tons and are used, among other things, for the production of abrasive powders.
The Uralgrit Group of Companies owns copper smelting slag dumps located in the cities of Karabash and Krasnouralsk, as well as nickel slag dumps located in Rezh, Orsk, and the urban-type settlement of Nikel.
Finished abrasive products are officially referred to by different names by various manufacturers, such as classified non-granulated slag, slag sand, abrasive sand, etc. Sometimes terms with geographical references are used, for example, “Karabash abrasives” or “Rezh abrasives.” These are not official trademarks but rather geographical identifiers of the production area and may be used by any abrasive manufacturer operating in that region.
At Uralgrit plants, both copper slag and nickel slag are produced — classified non-granulated slag under the Uralgrit brand.
Since 2024, the production of classified non-granulated slag based on copper smelting slag (copper slag) has been organized at the Uralgrit production site in Rezh, Sverdlovsk Region (Rezh Abrasive Plant).
The company’s products, regardless of the place of manufacture, have all the required certificates of conformity and quality passports for each batch.
Any manufacturers claiming that their region is the only place where copper slag is produced are misleading buyers and thereby bear administrative liability (Articles 14.7 and 14.33 of the Code of Administrative Offenses of the Russian Federation).
The claim that “genuine copper slag” can be purchased exclusively from a single manufacturer is false.

title: What Was the Level of Anti-Corrosion Protection (ACP) in the USSR? | Уралгрит
h1: What Was the Level of Anti-Corrosion Protection (ACP) in the USSR?
text:
On the Experience and Knowledge of Soviet Specialists
The experience and expertise of Soviet specialists are reflected in the anticorrosion library from the 1930s–1990s, compiled by Uralgrit.
In modern Russia, it is widely believed among anticorrosion protection (ACP) professionals that expertise in corrosion protection primarily belongs to Western companies, and that most practical knowledge has been adopted from specialists in Europe and the United States. This view is often supported by the fact that the Russian standard GOST R ISO 8501-1-2014 “Preparation of steel surfaces before application of paints and related products. Visual assessment of surface cleanliness” is based on the international standard ISO 8501-1:2007 “Preparation of steel substrates before application of paints and related products — Visual assessment of surface cleanliness.”
With regard to GOST standards—especially those related to corrosion protection systems—Soviet engineers did indeed rely on international standards.
However, a review of the extensive body of Soviet-era publications on corrosion protection—including textbooks, reference manuals, periodicals, and research papers—allows us to confidently state that USSR specialists had a deep understanding of what corrosion is, its causes, and the processes associated with it.
Did you know that in the USSR, up to 680 (!) hours were allocated for training a sandblaster? Such qualification enabled workers to understand the process in depth: what happens to the metal, where rust comes from, how to correctly select abrasives to achieve the required surface roughness profile, and much more. Today, the entry threshold to the profession is significantly lower, and many sandblasters perceive their task simply as “waving the nozzle,” without delving into the fundamentals of anticorrosion protection.
It is also worth noting that many so-called “modern” life hacks and surface protection recommendations were successfully used in the Soviet Union, while some effective corrosion prevention methods have been undeservedly forgotten.
For example:
All Soviet textbooks on ACP design took stray currents into account, with a primary focus on cathodic protection rather than paint and coating systems—whereas today this method is largely forgotten and rarely used.
Great attention was paid to metallization techniques—spraying zinc, aluminum, and stainless steel.
Instructions were provided on how to determine whether a metal surface was free from mill scale using copper sulfate (a “traditional” method). Modern GOST standards do not even provide a clear definition of “mill scale,” nor methods for proving its presence.
As early as the 1965–1970s, Soviet specialists wrote about the dangers of using quartz sand as an abrasive for blasting, although they were forced to work with quartz sand and shot due to the lack of alternatives. Information on the use of copper slag and nickel slag as abrasive blasting materials appears in literature from the 1990s—and it was during this period that Uralgrit became the first company in Russia to introduce these abrasive powders to the ACP market.
Over several decades, nothing fundamentally changed in abrasive blasting equipment—its design, operating principles, or components—except that it became more wear-resistant. Dustless blasting equipment was actively used in the USSR.
At Uralgrit, the library of publications from 1930–1990 continues to grow. Today, the collection includes more than 70 volumes. These books were intended for scientific and engineering professionals, designers, specialists from design and research institutes, university and technical college students, and were also used for professional training of industrial workers.

title: Black Spots After Abrasive Blasting | Уралгрит
h1: Black Spots After Abrasive Blasting
text:
Is the appearance of “black spots” on the surface during abrasive blasting considered a defect? What do you need to know to successfully pass inspection?
First, let’s refer to ISO 8501-1, the best reference for contractors regarding regulatory documentation that performers should rely on when presenting their work to the client.
First, the contractor must determine the initial degree of surface contamination – A, B, C, D. This is necessary to correctly use the reference surface later to check compliance with the cleaning degree specified in the project (for example, Sa2 or 2 1/2).
Depending on the initial contamination level (A, B, C, D), the reference surface for the cleaning degree (Sa2 or 2 1/2) will differ significantly!
A – smooth metal with continuous mill scale
B – presence of small pits
C – multiple pits with medium profile depth
D – multiple pits with deep profile
Referring again to ISO 8501-1, Sa2 or 2 1/2 means complete removal of mill scale, but the presence of black spots on a square decimeter (10×10 cm) is allowed up to 10.
So, what are black spots in our case?
Option 1: residues of mill scale or contaminants.
Why do they remain? If the surface contamination level is B, C, or D (not A), spots of contaminants may remain in existing metal pores because a large abrasive fraction was used (larger than the pits themselves). In the contact area during cleaning, the abrasive particle may not have reached the specific point in the pore (cleaning did not occur in this pit at a certain angle). Using a finer fraction eliminates this defect.
Option 2: “work-hardening” or metal transfer (“naklep”) – a component of copper slag (presence of other soft metals in the abrasive material) that embeds into the cleaned surface due to kinetic energy when striking a harder surface.
“Naklep” can be detected by visual inspection of the cleaned surface, possibly using a magnifying glass. The embedded particle can be removed mechanically using hand or power tools.
It occurs:
When air pressure in the blasting system is insufficient
When the attack angle on the surface is too direct
Increasing the air pressure and adjusting the attack angle eliminates these defects.
We thank Pavel Kusakin, expert at Uralgrit LLC, for assisting in preparing this material.

title: Disposal of Spent Nickel Slag and Copper Slag | Уралгрит
h1: Disposal of Spent Nickel Slag and Copper Slag
heads: Contractors performing abrasive blasting often face a requirement from the client to ensure disposal of spent material from the construction site. Let’s break down the key aspects of this issue.
text:
## Contractors performing abrasive blasting often face a requirement from the client to ensure disposal of spent material from the construction site. Let’s break down the key aspects of this issue.
Legal Grounds for Disposal Works
Contractors are often unsure which regulatory documents provide the basis for carrying out disposal works and receiving payment from the client.
In most cases, this requirement is stipulated in the contractual framework of the general contractor or the client. Frequently, this information is not communicated to the subcontractor—the direct executor of the works—and such activities are not reflected in the subcontract agreement or the attached cost estimate.
If the client demands disposal from a subcontractor, but this obligation is not предусмотрено by the contract, then such a requirement has no legal force and cannot be enforced.
Typically, disposal activities in the estimate are calculated based on transportation to the nearest landfill by geographic location. For example, if the nearest landfill is 40 km away, the estimate will specify removal of spent construction materials up to 40 km from the construction site.
Thus, if the contractor’s estimate includes collection of spent abrasive material and a logistics package for delivery to the nearest landfill with disposal, these works must be performed, and the contractor has grounds to receive payment.
Therefore, first of all, carefully review the contract to understand what exactly is required of you as the contractor:
cleaning, painting, and disposal
cleaning only,
cleaning and painting,
What Exactly Is Being Disposed Of
The first question a landfill representative will ask is: “What material are you disposing of?” In this case, it is spent slag — “slag after abrasive blasting,” waste code FKKO 36311111414.
It is critical to correctly classify and identify the waste hazard class in order to avoid overpaying for disposal. There are five hazard classes:
Class I — Extremely hazardous: causes irreversible environmental damage; no natural decomposition period.
Class II — Highly hazardous: severe ecosystem damage requiring at least 30 years for recovery after the source is removed.
Class III — Moderately hazardous: significant environmental damage, with recovery possible within about 10 years.
Class IV — Low hazard: harmful to nature, but recovery is possible within three years after disposal.
Class V — Practically non-hazardous: minimal impact on ecological balance; recovery may take less than three years.
Initially, classified ungranulated slag (copper slag and nickel slag), as a construction material, belongs to Hazard Class V (relatively safe).
After use, however, this material becomes spent material according to the Federal Waste Classification Catalogue (FKKO), i.e. construction waste. In theory, it can no longer be used on a construction site, as it becomes waste and no longer has a passport or quality certificate (see the article on Recuperation). According to the FKKO, it is assigned Hazard Class IV (average value).
A landfill operator may attempt to be “clever” and propose laboratory analysis, which creates a risk for the contractor that the waste will be classified as Hazard Class III, II, or even I—leading to a significant increase in disposal costs. A specific sample may deviate from averaged values (oil residues, paint residues, etc.). Therefore, it is generally advisable to refuse additional analysis and refer directly to the FKKO classification. The waste code is clearly defined, approved, regulated, included in the estimate, and paid accordingly.
Carrying Out Disposal Activities
Disposal begins with proper preparation of the work area. The contractor must install protective coverings, tarpaulins, or liners. These works and consumables should be included in the estimate. If they are not, the contractor performs them at their own expense, as they significantly facilitate collection of spent abrasive.
If no coverings are installed, collection can become extremely difficult. For example, if metal structures such as pipe racks are installed over crushed stone (70–90 mm fraction), the spent material falls between the stones and becomes hard to collect. In such cases, contractors may need to blow it out with compressed air, vacuum it, or wait for rain to wash it deeper between the stones.
Spent abrasive must be collected into piles rather than left as a thin layer scattered across the site.
Collection methods should be planned in advance:
Manual collection — shovels and wheelbarrows; suitable, for example, for tank interiors, where material can be removed through a manhole.
Mechanical collection — recovery units that can function like large industrial vacuum cleaners when suction hoses are repositioned.
Heavy equipment for large volumes — tractors pushing waste into piles, loading it into dump trucks, and transporting it away.
As a rule, logistics companies are available that can provide a full range of such services.
Case example (Krasnodar Krai, Rostov Region):
The estimate allowed 6,800 RUB per ton for disposal. A contractor was found who could arrive with loading equipment (excavator, front loader, dump trucks), perform loading, transportation to the landfill, and provide all reporting documents—for 2,000 RUB per ton . The difference became the contractor’s profit.
In some cases, the contractor must independently find a licensed landfill. More often, however, the contract already specifies the landfill and the distance to it. The contractor obtains a commercial proposal from the landfill and later receives official disposal documentation.
The contractor must report disposal activities to the client. The landfill provides closing documents—certificates of completed work, confirmation of accepted material, volume, and disposed hazard class.
Contracts usually specify the distance from the construction site to the landfill. Sometimes the client makes an error—for example, stating 40 km when the nearest landfill is actually 80 km away—resulting in additional logistics costs not accounted for in the estimate. However, the overall picture must be assessed, as the allocated logistics budget may still be sufficient despite the incorrect distance.
How to Calculate Waste Volume
Real case: A contractor delivered 100 tons of abrasive to a construction site, performed abrasive blasting of a tank, and removed 120 tons of waste. The client refused to pay for the additional 20 tons.
The client was correct. According to transport documents, a fixed amount of material was delivered based on the approved consumption rate. There are documents confirming delivery (waybills, checkpoint stamps for restricted facilities), which establish the allowable waste volume. If more waste is removed, it means the contractor also removed the client’s property—crushed stone, soil, debris, etc.
Therefore, the volume of disposed spent abrasive must not exceed the volume of delivered construction material. If 100 tons were delivered, no more than 100 tons should be removed.
Claims that the spent slag is “wet and heavier due to moisture” can be countered as follows: copper slag and nickel slag may theoretically absorb up to 3% surface moisture when exposed to rain, but the material is hydrophobic and does not absorb water internally. It cannot become significantly heavier due to moisture alone. Excess weight usually comes from foreign inclusions—soil, crushed stone, sand-gravel mix, clay—collected together with the slag. Such excess may be interpreted by the client as removal of their property.
Removal of a smaller volume of waste is permissible, although the client may question whether all waste was disposed of. It can be explained that during abrasive blasting, part of the crushed abrasive becomes airborne dust and may disperse up to 2–3 km depending on wind conditions.
However, if the estimate includes disposal of 100 tons and the contractor removes only 50 tons, payment will be made only for 50 tons. This results in lost potential income and unutilized budget under the contract.

title: Strength of Character | Уралгрит
h1: Strength of Character
text:
One of the meanings of the English term grit , along with “sand and gravel,” is “strength of character, courage, endurance.” This is remarkably accurate when applied to the Uralgrit Group of Companies, which recently celebrated its 25th anniversary in Yekaterinburg. Nadezhda Perevalova, General Director Uralgrit Group of Companies

The clear and coordinated work of all our structural divisions, the high-quality and timely fulfillment of assigned tasks, as well as favorable cooperation terms ensure high performance results and a leading position for the Uralgrit Group of Companies in a wide variety of markets.
We deliver a new level of strength.
There is much—indeed, very much—behind this, but it all began in the Sverdlovsk Region with loyalty… to the ruble, which became our lucky sign. We conclude deals in the national currency. And what is most interesting is that our partners in Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, Belarus, and practically everywhere else are increasingly asking us for this. We work wherever there is a technologically developed civilization, where there is a need to give a second life and a new level of strength and technical aesthetics to bridges, pipelines and gas pipelines, tanks, and in general to all critical products of modern industry.
A kind of industrial cleaning—only immeasurably more responsible.
Striving for Perfection as a Business Category
At a certain moment you suddenly realize that the best quality—even if it seems excessive to someone—is the key to tomorrow’s success. Your products and your managers must be the best on the market. And the company as a whole must also be the best. Because it is important to do everything for people in the best possible way.
Moreover, as an entrepreneur and industrialist with experience, I can state that our market itself does not require such total commitment. Many do not give their all, preferring to “go with the flow.” But if life (which, as we know, is given only once) and working at full capacity are interesting to you, if you are a perfectionist by nature, then only in this case will you get real pleasure from what you do every day, every hour, and every minute.
And when you are told, “Give us the price and to hell with the quality,” we must understand that by agreeing to this, each of us greatly impoverishes not only our own life but also the lives of other people. In other words, quality must be the best at a reasonable price. This is the Uralgrit principle.
Production Efficiency at Innoprom and in Life
Production efficiency is a component of the same quality. If you strive to make your product well and very well, then without efficient production this is impossible. And you should not be afraid to make something “too good”—if today’s consumer does not immediately appreciate it, the market itself will certainly appreciate it in the long term. The market clearly has a collective soul and mind and ultimately is our main judge when it comes to business. And the Russian person… attaches soul to everything.
Every segment of our business has been tested by time—engineers handle R&D, workers manage the production process, and marketers analyze the structure and dynamics of sales, ensuring feedback back into R&D.
The environmental aspect of our products is also noteworthy—over 25 years, responding to the wishes of environmentalists and customers, we have moved far ahead in terms of safety and environmental cleanliness of the abrasives produced by our company. We are pleased that builders, machine builders, and metallurgists are no longer threatened by silicosis and other once-occupational diseases. Thanks to our joint efforts, they have receded into the past, where they belong.
Caring about people turns out to be profitable. As a result, in marketing terms, a very interesting situation has developed in our abrasives market—the most expensive company also holds the largest market share. Ultimately, people, having “recovered” from the pursuit of cheapness, always return to quality.
The Demidovs as a Ural Beacon in Our Lives
We all grew up and work in the Urals, wherever our products are used. Therefore, we are sincerely inspired by the image of the Demidov industrialists, who created one of the world’s most successful (!) brands of the 18th century—“Old Sable.” We are proud of Tatishchev and De Gennin—the founders of the city where we live and work. How can we fail SUCH ancestors? After all, industrial culture is also transmitted at the genetic level. The team of our enterprise in every country where we operate confirms this “Not in words, but in deeds.” This is the motto of the Demidov family. And it lives on today.
Nadezhda Perevalova, General Director of Uralgrit Magazine “EXPO Sodruzhestvo,” June 2015

The “Tornado” nozzle was developed by technical experts of Uralgrit specifically for contractors performing abrasive blasting surface preparation.

Consumption per 1 sq. m is 3 kg (including a 30% loss factor). This is the actual consumption agreed with the client at the beginning of the project for this specific facility and material.
2
Cost of work: application of protective coating
1 sq. m = RUB 600 10,000 sq. m × RUB 600 = RUB 6,000,000
Painting rates depend on the region, client budget, individual agreements, and other factors.
3
Associated expenses: 3.1. Daily allowances 3.2. Accommodation 3.3. Consumables (nozzles, protective clothing) 3.4. Rental of painting equipment
1) 1 person = RUB 700/shift 11 people × RUB 700 × 90 days = RUB 693,000 2) 1 person = RUB 500/shift 11 people × RUB 500 × 90 days = RUB 495,000 3) RUB 300,000 4) 4 units × RUB 3,000/shift × 90 days = RUB 1,080,000
One month after the start of work, an auditor was invited to the site—a Level 3 protective coatings inspector from the Russian Register, with 15 years of experience, Pavel Valeryevich Kusakin .
At the time of the audit, the actual consumption of fire-protection material amounted to 4.2 kg per sq. m , which is 40% higher than the design value . By the inspector’s arrival, 25% of the planned area —2,500 sq. m—had been coated.
The material overspend was alarming— RUB 5.35 million , and going forward this figure could have increased fourfold !
The inspector was tasked with identifying the causes of excessive fire-protection material consumption and proposing solutions to optimize the process.
## The following causes of overspending were identified during the inspection:
The applicators did not measure WFT (wet film thickness) of the applied coating.
A hexagonal wet film gauge is used for these measurements.
2. The device for measuring DFT (dry film thickness) had not been verified or calibrated before measurements were taken. As a result, the readings did not reflect actual values.
The “Konstanta K-5” device was used for these measurements.
3. In addition, the workers lacked skills in using the measuring device and did not have sufficient theoretical knowledge.
There was no quality control personnel responsible for ensuring that coating thickness complied with the design specifications.
## To resolve the situation and prevent similar cases in the future, the following is recommended:
— Assign a quality control inspector (QC) to the site (salary approximately RUB 120,000 per month).
— Perform verification and calibration of the DFT measuring device (service cost approximately RUB 15,000).
— Train painters, foremen, site managers, and engineers under the programs “Painter” and “Painting Works Inspector” , including both theory and hands-on practice under the guidance of an experienced mentor (training cost is calculated upon request and depends on the number of trainees, site remoteness, duration of training, etc.).
## The Uralgrit Training Center (License No. 17105, series 66L01 dated 25.03.2013) provides 4–5 day training programs in the specialties “Abrasive Blaster”, “Industrial Painter”, and “Painting Works Inspector”, with on-site training at the client’s facility.
Training is conducted by an instructor certified by FROSIO, with 20 years of experience working at facilities of Rosneft, Transneft, Sibur, Lukoil, and Gazprom.
After completing the professional courses and reinforcing skills in practice, trainees take a qualification exam and receive a state-recognized certificate.

title: Abrasive Powder Recovery: Understanding the Issue | Уралгрит
h1: Abrasive Powder Recovery: Understanding the Issue
text:
In order to reduce abrasive material costs, both customers and contractors often raise the question of whether it is reasonable to use abrasive recovery systems directly at the job site.
More than 35 years of practical experience in abrasive blasting of steel structures using Uralgrit products (copper slag and nickel slag) has allowed us to summarize the experience of our partners and technical experts on this topic. We are sharing these insights with you.
Recovery systems are ideally suited for work performed in workshop conditions, for example, during the manufacturing of steel structures at fabrication plants.
However, when used at construction sites, a number of factors arise that negatively affect the process.
1. Possible Number of Reuse Cycles
In the case of copper slag, reuse is possible no more than twice.
In the case of nickel slag, reuse is not possible.
2. Changes in Abrasive Material Parameters
During blasting, the particle size of the recycled abrasive decreases due to the impact of particles against the steel surface. That is, if the original abrasive fraction was 0.5–2.5 mm, after recovery you will, at best, obtain a fraction of 0.2–1.6 mm, or even finer (depending on pressure, angle of impact, distance to the surface, etc.).
This leads to a mismatch with the surface roughness profile specified in the working or design documentation. As a result, the adhesion properties of the protective coating deteriorate, and the risk of warranty claims increases.
Abrasive losses are inevitable due to the wide dispersion radius of particles at the work site, as well as the ingress of foreign materials such as dust, debris, and other contaminants into the cleaning system.
The recycling process itself results in significant material losses—up to 60–70% of the input volume. In other words, from one ton of spent abrasive, no more than 300–400 kg of particles suitable for reuse will remain after recovery.
Spent abrasive particles absorb moisture, which leads to additional costs for drying, the need for extra drying equipment, and additional personnel.
The presence of mill scale residues, old paint coatings, traces of petroleum products, and other contaminants in the spent abrasive can increase the hazard class of waste after abrasive blasting to Class 4 or even Class 3 (depending on the type of contamination on the treated surface).
What Spent Copper Slag Looks Like
Below are illustrative photos showing spent copper slag: damp, containing debris inevitably present at construction sites, remnants of paint coatings, and chipped rust.
By contrast, high-quality abrasive material that ensures proper abrasive blasting quality is dry, clean, free of foreign inclusions, and has a clearly defined particle size distribution.
3. Practicality and Payback of Recovery Systems
Collecting spent abrasive requires additional labor costs , the involvement of extra personnel, and their training, which inevitably increases overall production costs.
Additional expenses will also arise for the purchase of recovery equipment and drying equipment (to eliminate moisture).
4. Certification of Recovered Abrasive
Uralgrit abrasive powder is fully certified during production: it undergoes laboratory testing and has standardized parameters (particle size distribution, moisture content, chemical composition, hazard class, etc.).
Each shipment is accompanied by the required documentation, including a certificate of conformity and a quality passport.
According to the Federal Waste Classification Catalogue (FKKO), spent abrasive particles are classified as construction waste and must be disposed of in accordance with their actual hazard class. The use of construction waste in production processes is not предусмотрено by legislation, contracts, or estimate documentation.
If you plan to perform abrasive blasting using self-recovered material, you are also responsible for obtaining all necessary permits for its use. This means you must prove that the material has been transformed back from construction waste into a construction material suitable for use as an abrasive. This requires laboratory test reports confirming its safety and suitability.
Documentation originally supplied with the abrasive material cannot be reused for the processed waste.
Conclusion
Under construction site conditions, where non-granulated slag abrasives (copper slag and nickel slag) are used, the application of abrasive recovery systems is impractical and economically unjustified.

title: Russian Waterjet Abrasive — Successful Import Substitution | Уралгрит
h1: Russian Waterjet Abrasive — Successful Import Substitution
text:
In 2017, two important EXPO events for the international economy took place in the territories of the two largest countries of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) — Russia and Kazakhstan: INNOPROM-2017 in Yekaterinburg (Russia) and EXPO-2017 in Astana (Kazakhstan). It is worth noting that the leading Russian company in the production of abrasive and waterjet abrasive materials in the Russian Federation, the EAEU, and the CIS — the Uralgrit Group of Companies — took part in both exhibitions.
The head of this Ural manufacturer, General Director of the Uralgrit Group of Companies Nadezhda Perevalova, talks about the innovative product the company will present at authoritative international exhibition forums.
Nadezhda Perevalova, General Director of Uralgrit Group of Companies
Nadezhda Perevalova, General Director of Uralgrit Group of Companies:
Russian Waterjet Abrasive — Successful Import Substitution
In the Year of Ecology in Russia, on the eve of the INNOPROM innovation forum in Yekaterinburg and the EXPO world exhibition in Astana dedicated to energy efficiency and conservation of natural resources, I am especially pleased to present the Russian import-substituting novelty — Uralgrit waterjet abrasive. The emergence of this material, developed by our specialists, became a kind of response to the calls of the President of Russia Vladimir Putin for more intensive implementation of the import substitution policy and the creation of a competitive domestic product capable of competing in international markets.
Thus, an entire import-substituting range of modern technologies for industrial cutting and processing of metals, alloys, rocks, and other materials using a large number of small solid particles supplied together with water under high pressure fully corresponds to the main trend of 2017 in Russia and in the world.
Challenge to the monopoly
Until recently, there were virtually no domestically produced waterjet abrasive materials on the Russian market. The main component of waterjet cutting for Russia (as, indeed, for the rest of the world) was “Garnet” — a material based on garnet sand, which today is almost entirely imported from distant India, Australia, and China and therefore has rather complex logistics for the Russian consumer.
In addition, the imported material is quite expensive — this is due to the need to deliver it from such fairly remote countries as India and Australia, as well as the risks of delivery disruptions, which occur quite often. All this places an additional burden on the cost of products in the manufacture of which garnet sand is used, as well as on the promptness of order fulfillment by domestic manufacturers.
Today the situation has changed fundamentally: consumables for waterjet cutting — currently the most environmentally friendly and energy-saving method of cutting and processing metals — are now produced by the Russian Uralgrit Group of Companies, which has been known on the market for almost 30 years as a manufacturer of abrasive materials for cleaning the surfaces of various critical materials.
Russian breakthrough
While working on the creation of Uralgrit waterjet abrasive, the company’s specialists faced the question of choosing a material that could become a full-fledged substitute for foreign competitors. It was important that the potential waterjet abrasive meet a whole set of requirements, such as particle hardness and cutting ability, the size of the resource base, environmental friendliness of the prospective production, and economic attractiveness for domestic industry.
After extensive research, the company’s specialists settled on copper slag, which is, in fact, a waste product of non-ferrous metallurgy. This is how, after the stage of working out technological solutions, the first Russian Uralgrit waterjet abrasive appeared.
I note that the domestic development is distinguished by a significantly wider range of applications compared with the same garnet sand. Suffice it to say that, unlike overseas competitors, our material can be produced in a greater number of fractions. For comparison, the particle size of garnet sand is fixed — from 0.1 to 0.6 mm. Narrower options — for example, from 0.1 to 0.3 mm — are not provided by either Indian or Australian manufacturers.
The range of fractions produced by the Uralgrit Group of Companies today is truly wide. In particular, one of the key plants of the Uralgrit Group of Companies in the city of Karabash, Chelyabinsk Region, can produce waterjet abrasive material with a fraction of absolutely any size depending on the customer’s wishes. For example — from 0.1 to 0.3 mm, or from 0.2 to 0.5 mm, or from 0.2 to 0.4 mm, etc., in any combinations.
Uralgrit waterjet abrasive: cuts effectively, cleans efficiently
The new material was subjected to a number of rigorous tests at production sites located throughout Russia. In particular, in the second quarter of 2017 alone, we conducted a set of comparative tests under industrial application conditions, including at the facilities of Blagoveshchensk Valve Plant JSC (Blagoveshchensk, April 2017), the company “Technologies of Precision Modeling” (Yekaterinburg, June 2017), and Robocat LLC (Tolyatti, June 2017).
These and other tests showed that the new Russian powder for waterjet cutting, Uralgrit, successfully cuts even such complex materials as thick natural granite and much more.
I note that the new product of Uralgrit can be used not only for cutting but also for cleaning various materials. Garnet sand and electrocorundum are also suitable for these purposes. However, the final cost of work using them in this capacity turns out to be much higher, and the fractional composition is largely fixed, which is a limiting factor, since it leads to a strictly defined and unchangeable surface roughness profile without post-processing. This is especially relevant for mechanical engineering and the oil and gas industry.
The unique properties of the Russian material were confirmed in 2016 during special tests in Bulanash in the Sverdlovsk Region. The Bulanash Machine-Building Plant located in this town specializes in the production of highly critical products — stainless steel caissons for the oil and gas industry. Using Uralgrit waterjet powder, stainless steel products were cleaned, after which the processed materials were transferred for study to the customer’s laboratory. The studies showed that Uralgrit waterjet abrasive indeed does not create preconditions for rust formation.
In addition, already in 2017, a separate cycle of tests of 80 mesh powder took place at the branch of Gazprom Dobycha Urengoy LLC (Novy Urengoy) — a subsidiary of the Russian oil and gas concern PJSC Gazprom. As part of the tests, the surface of one of the important elements of wellhead equipment — technological equipment used in gas production — was subjected to waterjet cleaning. The pilot use of the material confirmed the results obtained during previous tests and once again proved that the domestic waterjet abrasive powder 80 mesh is not inferior to imported garnet sand. This applies both to the processing speed of cleaned surfaces and to the quality and roughness profile.
After completing the test cycle, representatives of the subsidiary of the domestic oil and gas concern PJSC Gazprom stated that Uralgrit waterjet abrasive has the potential to become a full-fledged substitute for imported analogues in the Russian oil and gas industry.
In addition to successfully competing with “garnet,” the new domestic powder also confidently competes with another material widely used in abrasive cleaning — electrocorundum.
Thus, on April 19, 2017, in the presence of independent experts, comparative tests of the new Uralgrit material and electrocorundum were carried out in relation to the technology of “dry” abrasive surface cleaning. With the same fraction size in the range of 0.2–0.5 mm, both materials showed similar surface treatment quality — at the level of class “Sa 2.5.” The surface roughness profile of the surfaces treated by the “competitors” also turned out to be comparable: it varied within the range from 30 µm to 50 µm (microns). As a result of the tests, the specialists stated the identity of the obtained surface treatment results.
Alternative
In this sense, the new Uralgrit waterjet abrasive is a real alternative to imported materials — thanks to a greater number of particle size types, the Russian-made powder can be used for more thorough and higher-quality cleaning of the surfaces of critical products in domestic industry.
The cost of one minute of cutting with the Russian material is almost 30% lower than the price of the same minute of cutting using garnet sand. The reason for this lies in the savings due to the different cost of these waterjet abrasives and their performance characteristics. I also note an important aspect related, in a certain sense, to ensuring the country’s economic security.
First, the price list of our product is not “tied” to foreign currency exchange rates; therefore, it is stable and allows the manufacturer to plan the cost of its product over a much longer time interval. Logistics are also stable, since our partners do not need to accumulate large stocks of waterjet abrasive materials in warehouses and thereby withdraw significant financial resources from circulation for long periods. This also provides a considerable economic effect from cooperation with Uralgrit.
In this sense, Uralgrit waterjet abrasive is similar to a product on a supermarket shelf — it can be ordered exactly in the quantity needed at the moment. An order for the next batch of our product is always fulfilled on time, and the delivery process to the customer is always uninterrupted.
Buy garnet sand for waterjet cutting manufactured by Uralgrit
Secondly, today more than 1,000 waterjet installations operate in our country, which, according to experts, consume more than 29 thousand tons of abrasive materials per year. At the same time, almost half of consumers are located in the northwest and in the center of the country — where the main suppliers of “garnet” are also based.
The difficult economic situation in the country and the suspension of supplies from India that followed some time ago (which, according to experts, will last at least until September of the current year) have effectively forced Russian industry to look for an alternative. Everyone understands that if such an alternative does not exist, domestic plants may face serious difficulties, in the worst case — up to forced shutdowns of entire production sections with all the ensuing consequences.
At the same time, the alternative material must meet a whole range of requirements: similar quality and efficiency, more prompt and predictable delivery times, much lower and fixed cost for all regions of the country, and greater flexibility in supply volumes. Uralgrit waterjet abrasive, which is produced practically in the center of Russia, acts as such an import-substituting material.
Uralgrit waterjet abrasive: an invitation to the future
Today, the Uralgrit Group of Companies is working to fully satisfy the growing demand for domestic waterjet abrasive in the markets of the Volga, Ural, and Siberian regions, in Kazakhstan, and in other countries of Central Asia. All this is being done so that the new Russian material, so convenient for our manufacturers in every respect, becomes more accessible and widespread, which in the future will make it possible to further reduce consumer costs and make Russian products competitive in global markets.

text:
Uralgrit LLC has been operating in the market since 1988. The group of companies provides a full range of services in the field of anticorrosion protection. The clear and coordinated work of all structural divisions, high-quality and timely fulfillment of assigned tasks, as well as favorable cooperation terms ensure high performance results and a leading position in the market.
Alexandra Leonidovna Chervotkina, Head of Sales Department of Uralgrit LLC, told us about the company’s activities.
Alexandra Leonidovna Chervotkina, Head of Sales Department Uralgrit Group of Companies
Company name. How was it created?
Uralgrit LLC has held leading positions in the market for more than 25 years. The company name comes from the combination of the words Ural and grit, which translated from English means sand, crumb.
Business focus. Which markets does the company target? Are there representatives in regions and countries?
The company’s priority business area is anticorrosion protection of metal and metal structures. Among its clients are the largest enterprises in ship repair, shipbuilding, oil and gas, and construction industries from Russia and CIS countries. To maximize customer satisfaction, a wide network of its own warehouses and representative offices has been created and is constantly expanding. Today, abrasive powder under the Uralgrit brand can be purchased throughout Russia as well as in the Republic of Belarus, Azerbaijan, and Kazakhstan.
Are there exclusive products in your range? How do they differ from competitors’ offerings?
Uralgrit was the first to propose using nickel powder (nickel slag) for fast and efficient cleaning of large open surfaces such as ship hulls. Abrasive particles, striking the surface, chip off small pieces of rust, scale, and old paint coatings while simultaneously “undermining” the coating in adjacent areas, which ensures high cleaning speed.
To solve the problem of reducing the dust cloud during cleaning in confined spaces, a coarse fraction of copper slag was developed, characterized by increased dynamic strength, whose particles do not break upon impact with the treated surface.
The company offers a wide fraction range that meets various customer needs in anticorrosion surface protection and is actively expanding the application areas of Uralgrit abrasive powder.
Products under the Uralgrit brand compare favorably with competitors due to their stable fractional composition, high degree of cleaning that reduces dust cloud formation during surface treatment, and significant cost savings with higher productivity.
How do you promote your company?
We have chosen online advertising, advertising on major industry internet portals, and periodically publish in particularly significant industry print media. We consider participation in exhibitions of the shipbuilding, oil and gas, and construction industries to be an effective type of promotion.
Are there long-term employees in your team? What is the average tenure in the company? The company in faces. Is there an employee whose example could illustrate the company’s development path?
Of course, as in any company, there is staff rotation, but we are proud that the company’s key specialists—its driving force—stay with us for many years. For example, Chief Engineer Sergey Pavlovich Yakovlev has been working with the company for 15 years. The example of Ivan Sergeevich Bespalov is also illustrative: he joined the plant as an ordinary worker and, having gone through all stages, became the director of the Uralgrit plant in Karabash (Chelyabinsk Region).
The axis of our company is N.V. Perevalova—a professional, charismatic, and competent director. Thanks to her balanced decisions and ability to unite the team, we all work as one unit, achieving our goals.
Great attention is paid to the development of corporate culture, and broad opportunities are provided for the growth and development of each employee.
How do you assess the market situation and your competitors? Are you an industry leader or still fighting for leadership positions?
We are a leader in the surface anticorrosion protection industry. Of course, we have to share market space with our main competitors, who are also actively developing at the moment. However, we do not consider this a negative factor, because healthy competition is the “engine of progress.” Its presence does not allow us to rest on our laurels; it encourages us to set more ambitious goals and seek entry into new markets.

title: Uralgrit Hydroabrasives — Closer to the Customer | Уралгрит
h1: Uralgrit Hydroabrasives — Closer to the Customer
heads: Uralgrit Hydroabrasives — Closer to the Customer
From Nickel Slag to Copper Slag
text:
Today, Uralgrit rightfully embodies the goals of import substitution in Russia, as the well-known Ural manufacturer has become a pioneer in creating a modern domestic hydroabrasive production industry. Nadezhda Perevalova, CEO of the Uralgrit Group of Companies, explains how the company is developing this new technology.
Nadezhda Perevalova, CEO of the Uralgrit Group of Companies
Choose Russian!
## Uralgrit Hydroabrasives — Closer to the Customer
The principle of hydroabrasive application has been known for hundreds of years. The original Greek term abrasive means “to scrape,” while the prefix hydro means “water.” Thus, the word “hydroabrasive” literally translates as “scraping with water.” In ancient Greek civilization, the term was associated with hide cleaning; today it describes a wide range of modern industrial technologies for cutting and processing metals, alloys, rocks, and other materials using a large number of fine hard particles supplied with water under high pressure.
Until recently, there were virtually no domestically produced materials of this type on the Russian market. The primary hydroabrasive used in Russia (as in the rest of the world) has been garnet—a material based on garnet sand that is almost entirely imported from India, Australia, and China.
Put simply, the main advantage of garnet is its natural origin: manufacturers only need to mine it, bag it, and ship it to customers. However, consumers of this exotic product are well aware of its significant drawbacks. The key issue is the fixed particle size (also naturally determined), typically ranging from 0.1 to 0.6 mm. As a result, the surface roughness profile of the processed part is essentially fixed and cannot be adjusted. As manufacturing increasingly demands higher precision, additional post-processing becomes necessary, leading to extra energy and resource consumption.
In short, reducing costs with garnet is difficult—especially given its dependence on sea delivery from India and Australia and its high price. All of this increases production costs and affects delivery timelines for domestic manufacturers, since the material is literally overseas and subject to frequent and lengthy supply disruptions.
Today the situation has changed dramatically. Consumables for hydroabrasive cutting—currently the most environmentally friendly and energy-efficient method of metal cutting and processing—are now produced by the Ural-based Uralgrit Group, long known for its abrasive materials for critical surface preparation. The company will celebrate its 30th anniversary next year and continues expanding into new markets and regions.
It is therefore unsurprising that the price of the first Russian hydroabrasive turned out to be significantly lower than imported analogues. Reliable delivery is also ensured: the new Uralgrit hydroabrasive is produced in the heart of the country and delivered by rail or truck.
## From Nickel Slag to Copper Slag
One of the first products of the Ural abrasive industry was a powder based on nickel slag. However, it could only serve as a full replacement for garnet within a limited range of applications. Nickel slag particles are much more brittle than those of garnet sand or fused alumina.
Therefore, our specialists set out to find a material capable of fully replacing imported hydroabrasives. After extensive research, copper slag —with virtually inexhaustible reserves—was selected. This led to the creation of the first Russian hydroabrasive, 80 mesh.
Industrial tests conducted by Uralgrit in March 2017 at the Blagoveshchensk Valve Plant showed that the new 80-mesh hydroabrasive cutting powder matches imported competitors from India and Australia in quality, efficiency, and application methods. For example, the Russian hydroabrasive cuts steel up to 40 mm thick just as effectively as garnet—and performs even better and cleaner on polymers.
Another key advantage of the new Russian product is the ability to manufacture a wider range of particle sizes. By comparison, garnet sand has a fixed size range of 0.1–0.6 mm. Narrower ranges (for example, 0.1–0.3 mm) are not offered by Indian or Australian producers, nor specified in domestic technical standards.
Thanks to the 2016 modernization of one of our key plants in Karabash (Chelyabinsk Region), Uralgrit can produce hydroabrasive material in virtually any fraction size according to customer requirements—for example: 0.1–0.3 mm, 0.2–0.5 mm, 0.2–0.4 mm and many other combinations
This approach is highly advantageous for domestic industry, as it allows customers to order the exact fraction optimal for cutting specific materials. The quality of the 80-mesh abrasive enables customers to produce end products that require little or no additional finishing.
For our partners, this means reduced time, financial, and labor costs—an essential benefit in today’s challenging business environment.
The new Uralgrit abrasive can be used not only for cutting but also for surface cleaning. Garnet sand and fused alumina can also perform these tasks, but at significantly higher cost. Moreover, their fixed particle size limits achievable surface roughness without post-processing.
In contrast, the broader particle size range of Uralgrit abrasives enables more thorough and higher-quality surface cleaning—especially important for mechanical engineering and the oil and gas industry.
For example, Uralgrit abrasive powder can be used to clean stainless steel without risking corrosion. The particles, which contain metal oxides, do not remain on the treated surface. Therefore, no oxide film forms, eliminating the risk of subsequent corrosion—an important advantage in aggressive oil and gas environments.
These properties were confirmed in 2016 during special tests in Bulanash (Sverdlovsk Region). The Bulanash Machine-Building Plant, which produces critical stainless-steel caissons for the oil and gas industry, verified that Uralgrit hydroabrasive leaves no oxide film and does not create conditions for rust formation.
Skeptics may note that many other cutting technologies exist today—plasma, laser, waterjet, and others. However, each has its own limitations. Laser and plasma cutting cause edge melting and heat-affected zones, often requiring mandatory post-processing. Pure water cutting involves high water consumption and extremely high pressure, increasing energy use. Against the global trend toward energy efficiency, hydroabrasive cutting is gaining increasing attention. It is one of the fastest-growing material cutting technologies and a serious competitor to plasma, laser, and traditional machining.
A hydroabrasive jet is essentially an ideal cutting tool with no wear. The jet diameter ranges from 0.5 to 1.5 mm, minimizing waste. Cutting can begin at any point along even highly complex contours. Materials from 0.1 mm up to 300 mm thick (or more) can be processed.
This makes hydroabrasive cutting indispensable in: mechanical engineering, tool manufacturing, aerospace, defense and transport engineering, stone processing.
Another major advantage is the absence of thermal and deformation effects. Physical, chemical, and mechanical properties of the material remain unchanged. No heating at the cut zone also ensures full fire safety and eliminates toxic fumes.
Some materials—ceramics, composites, multilayer and honeycomb structures—can currently be processed only by hydroabrasive methods.
There are currently about 1,200 hydroabrasive machines operating in Russia, half of them located in the Northwest and Central regions—where the main garnet suppliers are also based. Until recently, users had little choice but to purchase imported garnet.
However, the challenging economic environment and supply disruptions from India have forced Russian industry to seek alternatives with: comparable quality, shorter delivery times, stable nationwide pricing flexible supply volumes.
Uralgrit hydroabrasive, produced in central Russia, serves as this alternative.
Price is influenced, among other factors, by packaging. Indian and Australian suppliers ship only in 25-kg bags. Uralgrit offers both: 25-kg bags and big bags up to 1 ton
For example:
1 ton in one big bag: 18,000–20,000 RUB (incl. VAT)
1 ton in 25-kg bags on pallets: about 22,000 RUB (incl. VAT)
The difference may seem small, but at large volumes it results in significant savings. Additionally, due to long logistics routes, imported abrasives are almost 30% more expensive than the Russian analogue.
The new domestic material is also undergoing certification for use on both imported (primarily Chinese and Czech) and Russian equipment, making the product universal.
Today, the Uralgrit Group is expanding its presence in the Volga, Ural, and Siberian regions, as well as Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries. The company is also targeting southern Russia.
To move closer to customers, a new nickel-based abrasive plant has been built in Orsk (Orenburg Region), and the company is considering a new copper-based hydroabrasive facility in Krasnouralsk (Sverdlovsk Region).
Government authorities actively support domestic manufacturers, including Uralgrit, through state orders and partnership programs.
At the same time, occupational safety remains an important issue. In 2012, Russia’s Chief Sanitary Doctor Gennady Onishchenko approved standards stating that quartz sand should not be used for abrasive blasting due to the risk of silicosis and lung cancer.
However, existing construction standards still often fail to distinguish between traditional silica-containing materials and innovative Uralgrit abrasives, which contain no quartz sand and therefore do not pose a silicosis risk.
Although Uralgrit hydroabrasive does contain a dust fraction that may be inhaled, it is naturally eliminated from the body.
Environmental authorities also warn about the risks of traditional quartz abrasives in bridge work due to potential water contamination. Uralgrit abrasive and hydroabrasive materials can be safely used at water facilities because they contain neither free silicon nor silicon dioxide.
In our view, solving these issues requires coordinated involvement of regulators, industry, builders, environmental specialists, and medical experts. Positive progress would improve environmental safety in cutting and cleaning processes and reduce occupational cancer risks—matters of both economic and national security.
Overall, despite certain challenges, we remain optimistic. The domestic hydroabrasive industry has every chance to become an important part of Russia’s economy and take another step into the future.

title: Sandblasting machine: how it works, layout, types | Уралгрит
h1: Sandblasting machine: how it works, layout, types
heads: What is a sandblasting machine? Main parameters of sandblasting equipment
Types of sandblasting machines, features of their operation
Tips and criteria for choosing a sandblaster
text:
## What is a sandblasting machine? Main parameters of sandblasting equipment
A sandblasting machine is a pressure vessel into which abrasive material is poured. In terms of volume, this equipment comes in 25-liter, 50-liter, 100-liter, and 200-liter sizes. Sandblasting machines are also available with or without remote control.
These machines are used in enclosed spaces and open areas. The machines themselves cannot be lifted, so in this case, the length of the hose and the number of abrasive blasting hoses are increased.
## Key parameters of sandblasting equipment
When choosing an abrasive blasting machine, the following parameters must be taken into account:
Pressure — range up to 10 atmospheres.
Volume of the tank for mixing air with abrasive — 25, 50, 100, 200 liters. The larger the tank volume, the longer you can work without stopping.
A sandblasting machine consists of the following main components:
Tank for abrasive material.
Sieve and cover.
Moisture and oil separator filter: necessary to keep the abrasive material dry and free from moisture, oil, and other impurities.
Dosing valve: necessary for pressure regulation.
Remote control unit with remote control.
Double hose and hose fittings.
Sometimes a receiver is placed separately between the compressor and the sandblasting machine. This is a vessel in which compressed air is accumulated, consumed, and stored. It is designed to make the compressor work more efficiently.
The principle of operation of an abrasive blasting machine is that abrasive material is supplied under pressure from the nozzle, which cleans the working surface. Let’s take a closer look:
Air from the compressor is fed into the machine through a high-pressure compressed air hose.
Abrasive material is poured into the tank and mixed with air.
Then the abrasive (of a certain fraction and type) is fed from the tank through the abrasive blasting hose into the nozzle.
## Sandblasting machine connection layout
A compressor that supplies air through a compressed air hose.
It is connected to couplings that connect the hose to the compressor.
An abrasive blasting hose runs from the sandblasting machine and is also connected by a coupling, a nozzle holder, and a nozzle.
The second line goes to the sandblaster:
A compressed air hose runs from the compressor to the breathing air filter.
Then there is a hose that connects the filter to the helmet and supplies air to the sandblaster’s helmet.
The device must be equipped with a metering valve. They come in the following types:
slide gate (or abrasive blasting) type in the form of a disc, suitable for abrasive materials (copper slag, nickel slag, sand);
shot blasting type;
valves in the form of a tee, which are designed for use with shot.
The valve is necessary to regulate the pressure, which directly affects the consumption of abrasive material when the compressor is started (when the abrasive blasting machine is turned on).
If the dispenser is not adjusted, it will be fully open, which leads to:
increased abrasive consumption;
increased roughness of the surface being cleaned;
pressure loss.
If there is no remote control, there must be a second operator who is constantly present at the machine. The sandblaster himself is located directly at the surface being treated and does not move around the object during operation. The equipment is started/stopped by the second operator at the machine.
## Areas of application
Sandblasting machines are used in various fields. Main areas of application:
Metallurgy.
Oil and gas industry.
Industrial construction.
Shipbuilding and ship repair.
Bridge construction.
Service stations and auto repair shops.
Sandblasting of glass and mirrors.
## Types of sandblasting machines, features of their operation
Surface treatment machines are classified according to several criteria. Each has its own differences and characteristics. The main classification method is based on the method of abrasive delivery:
Ejector – a non-sealed container that is not pressurized during use; the performance of such equipment is several times lower.
Pressure type – the container is pressurized; this type of machine provides the highest productivity.
## What abrasives should be used?
In order for sandblasting equipment to perform its functions, it is necessary to select the right abrasive powders. The most popular abrasives used for this work are:
Copper slag (copper production waste);
Nickel slag (nickel production waste);
Restoration powder (copper slag of a very fine fraction of 0.0-0.2 mm for delicate cleaning);
Hydroabrasive (when working with soft metal alloys);
Garnet sand, etc.
Quartz sand is still used, despite the fact that its use causes the dangerous disease “silicosis” and is prohibited in sandblasting work in accordance with SP 2.2.2.1327-03 “Hygienic requirements for the organization of technological processes, production equipment, and working tools.”
When using abrasive materials, it is important to pay attention to the dispensers used in the device. If abrasive powders are used, slide gate dispensers must be used, and if shot is used, shot blasting dispensers must be used.
Copper slag is used in enclosed spaces, as when it hits the surface, the copper slag particles do not break, but deform, and therefore the dust level is reduced. Nickel slag has a higher cleaning speed and is used in open areas.
The abrasive blaster selects the appropriate type of abrasive material for a specific task. For example, if a tank needs to be cleaned, the inside is cleaned with copper slag and the outside with nickel slag.
## Safety precautions
Since sandblasting equipment poses a health hazard, safety precautions must be observed when working with it, in particular:
Sandblasters must wear specialized clothing: sturdy shoes, overalls, gloves, and a helmet that completely covers the face and eyes. A respirator with filters and noise-canceling headphones must be used.
Before using the equipment, read the instructions for the sandblasting machine.
Pay attention to the suitability of the abrasive material used for cleaning (it is important to use only dry abrasives!) and the equipment settings.
If the surface cleaning work is carried out at a height or far from the machine, a remote control must be used, as it is not possible to walk around the site with the nozzle switched on.
The nozzle should only be directed at the area to be cleaned.
Do not perform sandblasting work with worn or damaged equipment.
## Tips and criteria for choosing a sandblaster
Understand the scope of work and where it will be carried out.
Pay attention to the selection of the compressor so that it provides the necessary pressure.
Study the customer’s technical specifications.
Pay attention to the nozzle diameter – for the correct choice, multiply the size of the maximum abrasive particle by 4. For example, if we have a fraction of 0.5-1.5, then this is a nozzle with a diameter of 6 mm. If the nozzle is selected incorrectly, there will be significant wear on the equipment, clogging or a decrease in cleaning quality and performance is possible.
Pay attention to the couplings (nylon or metal). Nylon is less durable.
When setting up the machine, it is necessary to take into account the fraction of the abrasive used.
Power level. The indicators must be able to cope with the planned task.
Dimensions, mobility. It is necessary to understand the purpose for which the equipment is being purchased and how often it will need to be moved.
Study all the technical characteristics of the equipment.
It is recommended to give preference to sandblasting equipment from official manufacturers and avoid “homemade” equipment, which is potentially dangerous in the production process.
The financial aspect is also an important factor. If you have no experience, it is better to consult a specialist.

title: Customer Experience with Uralgrit Restoration Powder | Уралгрит
h1: Customer Experience with Uralgrit Restoration Powder
heads: Compatibility with conventional abrasive blasting equipment

text:
Uralgrit restoration powder is a fine-fraction abrasive (0.001–0.2 mm) produced from non-granulated slags on high-precision equipment in limited volumes. It provides a surface roughness profile of 5–10 μm, is used for delicate blasting and sweeping, and enables gentle abrasive cleaning of metal, plastic, stone, brick, wood, non-ferrous metals, and other types of surfaces.
Over more than five years of sales, the restoration powder has gained recognition among consumers. This review of the material’s application features is based on user experience — real customer reviews from marketplaces and surveys of users who purchased the abrasive from the manufacturer’s warehouse were used.
## Advantages and application features
## Effective surface preparation
“Good abrasive, cleans pores as much as possible due to the very fine fraction, cleans very softly and delicately.”
“Very fine and processes the surface efficiently.”
“Handles light rust perfectly.”
“Either I chose the wrong fraction, or it didn’t suit my task. It cleans well, but not deep rust.”
“Suitable for removing rust, but it won’t remove a thick layer of paint, or at least I couldn’t do it with a sandblasting gun. A very delicate material.”
“Cleans better than sand.”
Thanks to its unique fractional composition, Uralgrit restoration powder penetrates well into localized pitting corrosion zones, cleans hard-to-reach areas, removes contaminants in pores, and provides the required level of cleaning and surface preparation for subsequent application of protective coatings.
It is especially recommended in situations when:
— the surface had previously been prepared, but over time the metal developed secondary light corrosion and gentle blasting is required;
— corrosion remains in pores due to a large roughness profile;
— after passing through the dew point outdoors, the peaks remained clean while rust appeared inside the cavities (secondary corrosion), making surface sweeping necessary.
## Delicate impact
“Cleans gently; for rough cleaning it’s too fine.”
“Fine abrasive for delicate cleaning, coarse abrasive for rough cleaning.”
“One advantage is that it doesn’t overheat the metal.”
“Perfect for restoration.”
“Excellent abrasive for delicate work. Especially for a mini gun.”
The fine fraction with minimal variation in particle size ensures a delicate effect on the surface while preserving its integrity and original appearance, which is especially important in restoration work.
Due to the reduced specific weight of the particles, the dynamic impact of the abrasive on the surface is minimized—an impact that can otherwise cause destruction of an existing protective coating. The restoration powder is effective for layer-by-layer removal of old coatings and for cleaning the top layer, as it does not create internal stress in the coating.
## Compatibility with conventional abrasive blasting equipment
“Excellent. Bought it for a mini SandJet sandblaster. Works one hundred percent.”
“Compatible with MaxJet.”
“Works great with the SandJet sandblaster.”
“Cleans normally. Bought it for SandJet.”
“For SandJet it’s a killer.”
“SandJet works perfectly with this abrasive.”
“The abrasive is ideal for industrial use. It can also be used in a restoration workshop even with a miniature sandblaster, but it is demanding in operation.”
For small volumes of work in a workshop with a small sandblasting cabinet and SandJet or MaxJet sandblasting guns, Uralgrit restoration powder will be an optimal choice.
When working with more professional and high-performance equipment such as Contracor, Graco, PST (Pnevmostroytekhnika), Vector, etc., it is important to adjust the settings to achieve the desired result: reduce the nozzle diameter to 6 mm or less, lower the pressure starting from 1 atm, and change the angle of attack.
## The need to use personal protective equipment
“You need thick rubber gloves and a respirator, because dust from the fine fraction is present, especially when reused.” “You need thick rubber gloves and a respirator, because dust from the fine fraction is present, especially when reused.”
“Simply great! Work only with PPE!”
The use of PPE (a helmet or protective goggles, mask, sandblasting suit) to protect the respiratory system from dust is mandatory when using any abrasives, especially when working with fine fractions, since dust formation will be increased.
Reuse of spent abrasive is not recommended by the manufacturer—see the article “Recovery of abrasive powder: understanding the issue” for more details.
## High abrasive quality
“Good slag, an order of magnitude less dust, I recommend it.”
“Excellent copper slag, dry, fractionated.”
“The copper slag is dry, a pleasure to work with.”
“Everything is great. Excellent product! I recommend it!”
Uralgrit restoration powder is produced in full compliance with technical specifications (TU). The content of the working fraction is strictly controlled—samples are taken on an ongoing basis by the Quality Control Department engineers. The packaging meets all necessary requirements to protect against moisture ingress.
## Variety and convenience of packaging
“Many thanks to the seller. Perfectly sealed!”
“5 kg is of course not much, but for processing small parts / surfaces it’s excellent.”
“I really liked this product, thanks to the seller. I recommend it!”
The main type of packaging is an FIBC (big bag) weighing 1 ton, with two lifting loops. It has additional protection against ultraviolet exposure and a double inner liner to ensure tightness. After opening, the remaining abrasive should be stored in a dry room.
Small packaging is available in the following formats:

heads: Photo of paving tiles using slag
text:
Are you looking for a way to reduce the cost of paving tiles without losing strength, or do you want to achieve a premium “granite-like” texture without using expensive pigments? Nickel slag is a solution that technologists have been using for a long time, but they do not always disclose the proportion secrets. Let’s examine how to properly introduce the abrasive powder into production, why only the 0.8–3.0 mm fraction is suitable, and how to avoid defects.
## Why nickel slag?
Nickel only: Only nickel slag is suitable for paving tiles. Copper smelting slag (copper slag) often gives a reddish tint or has a different density, which is critical for the decorative layer.
Stone aesthetics:The black glossy sheen of the slag imitates natural stone. This makes it possible to save on colorants while achieving a noble dark shade.
## Technology: Two-layer molding
It is important to understand: slag is an additive for the textured (face) layer.
Fraction matters: Use strictly 0.8–3.0 mm. A finer fraction will “sink” into the cement paste and will not provide a visual effect, while a coarser fraction may reduce flexural strength.
Raw material cleanliness: The main enemy of quality is dust. In our slag, dust-like particles have been removed. The presence of dust sharply increases the water demand of the mixture, which leads to reduced frost resistance of the product.

title: Slag for road filling | Уралгрит
h1: Slag for road filling
heads: Use of copper slag for road filling
text:
Copper slag is a product of non-ferrous metallurgy. It is used not only as an abrasive powder for sandblasting, but also for filling road and building foundations. Uralgrit supplies material with a fraction of up to 10 mm in bags with delivery to any region, as well as in bulk for self-pickup from factories.
## Material characteristics
Slag is obtained during the smelting of copper ores. When cooled rapidly, it acquires a glassy structure that is dense and durable. It contains minerals that provide high mechanical strength and stable behavior under loads.
The compressive strength of copper smelting slag reaches 140 MPa, while that of porous slag is about 62 MPa.
The density is higher than that of granite crushed stone, and the material is not hygroscopic. Due to its high water permeability, slag quickly dries the surface and does not retain water.
The average consumption rate is about 1.4–1.6 tons per 10 m² with a layer thickness of 10 cm.
The moisture content of copper slag and nickel slag shipped in big bags, which have high-strength packaging and a double liner, is no more than 0.2%. It is also possible to ship the abrasive in bulk.
## Use of copper slag for road filling
Copper slag is used in the construction of temporary and permanent road surfaces. The main areas of its use in road construction are as follows:
On soft or loose soils, slag is used as a filler. This prevents the soil from being washed away and improves its ability to bear the weight of structures or passing vehicles.
When building temporary or technological roads, copper slag is used instead of ordinary crushed stone. It becomes a solid foundation on which concrete is then poured.
Copper slag is used for road filling at factories and construction sites. It is quickly compacted and does not wash away with water during rain.
